anchors.fact: Born Gladys Louise Smith. When Belasco cast her at 15 he recommended a more star-like name. "Mary Pickford" came from a surname in her mother's family and a fib: she told him her middle name was Marie, not Louise, then turned it into Mary. The page doesn't say who picked "Pickford". (PBS, P4)
anchors.meaning: Even the name was put together.

anchors.fact: The public called her "America's Sweetheart" and "the Girl with the Golden Curls"; fans said "our Mary". (PBS, P1; Regan, *Joy* pdf 341, "America's Sweetheart")
anchors.meaning: The wanting came with names other people gave her.

anchors.fact: She saw that film needed a new kind of acting: smaller, more intimate, with the feeling in the eyes, not in big gestures. (PBS, P6)
anchors.meaning: The effect was worked out, not luck.

anchors.fact: Griffith offered five dollars a day, three days a week. She asked for ten a day and more for extra work, and he agreed. She kept moving company for higher pay, with her mother's encouragement. (PBS, P5, P7)
anchors.meaning: She named her price, and got it.

anchors.fact: In 1919 she and three other filmmakers (Chaplin and Griffith among them) founded United Artists, to distribute their own films and break the distributors' hold on the money. She called the satisfaction, in a word, freedom. (PBS, P8)
anchors.meaning: She built the structure so the work stayed hers to run.

anchors.fact: Her own company's money needs pressed her into the roles her fans loved; *Pollyanna* (1920) fixed the little-girl image even harder. (PBS, P9)
anchors.meaning: The trap was the success: the thing she built kept her in the curls.

anchors.fact: In 1928, the year her mother died, she cut off the famous curls, and fans attacked her for it. She said later it was as if she'd killed someone, but only so the one who came next could live. (PBS, P10; her motive on record is grief plus that line, C6)
anchors.meaning: She ended the image so the person after it could live. Any "strategy" reading is ours, signposted.

anchors.fact: A Prohibition-era drink of white rum, pineapple and a little grenadine was named for her. By one 1928 account a Havana bartender made it for her visit, most likely in December 1922. Reportedly one of the three most-ordered drinks in Cuba then. (Oxford pdf 1252; maker contested, C1)
anchors.meaning: The drink was made for the famous face.
anchors.speaksTo: the tie (Wren): that one for the star, this one for the one running things

anchors.fact: No page says she drank it. Two library books name two different makers (Kaufman, Oxford/Woon; Woelke, Regan), so no maker's name in guest text. Oxford's own recipe has no maraschino; its MARASCHINO entry and Regan's have it, so no "original recipe". (C1–C5)
anchors.meaning: Keep the drink lines to "named for her".

anchors.fact: Bacardi set up in Puerto Rico in 1936 and left Cuba after the revolution; today's bottle isn't made in Havana. (Oxford BACARDI pdf 182)
anchors.meaning: "The rum the drink's entry names" is true; "the same rum" isn't.

cocktail.closingLine: Make the grenadine yourself, the day before. Then choose your next version before anyone asks for the old one.
method: The day before, make the grenadine. In a clean jar put 250 g of pomegranate juice (100% juice), 250 g of white sugar and 6 sprigs of thyme, crushed lightly in your hand. Close the lid and shake until the sugar has dissolved, which takes a few minutes. Leave it in the fridge overnight, then strain out the thyme. It keeps about a week in the fridge.
Put a cocktail glass in the freezer.
Measure the rum, pineapple, lime and 2½ teaspoons (12.5 ml) of the grenadine into a shaker.
Fill the shaker three-quarters with ice and shake hard until the outside is too cold to hold. The pineapple will foam a little, and it should.
Strain into the cold glass. No garnish.
cocktail.name: By Design

recipe.note: unaged or lightly aged, not spiced or sweetened; labelled 50% ("100 proof" in the US) or a little stronger; anything from 50% to 63% works
homemade, the day before: pomegranate juice, sugar and thyme (see Method)

cocktail.tagline: Everyone knows the effect you have. Almost nobody knows you designed it.

reading.epigraph: Named in Havana for America's Sweetheart. This one's for the one behind the curls.
whoYouAre: You know what you do to people, because you worked it out. The voice, the pause before you answer, the one thing everyone remembers you wore: none of it is an accident, and you'd be quietly proud if anyone asked. They don't. They think you were simply born like that.

People fall for what you made. Very few ask to meet the one who made it. That part is lonely, and you almost never mention it, because to everyone else it seems like having it all. And when you're steering, with no credit for it, an evening can turn warm, even daring, and never tip into trouble. People feel more alive around you, and safe. That's care too, though it looks like a show.
yours: Before she was America's Sweetheart, she was Gladys Smith. A producer suggested a more star-like name, so one was made, partly from a fib about her middle name. When D. W. Griffith offered her five dollars a day, she asked for ten, and got it.

In 1919, with Chaplin, Griffith and others, Mary Pickford founded United Artists, so its founders could distribute their own films. The satisfaction, she said, was in one word: freedom. Then the twist: the company needed money, and the money was in the girl with the golden curls. The thing she built to be free kept her in them.

In 1928, the year her mother died, Pickford cut them off. Her fans were scathing. Looking back, she said people reacted as if she'd killed someone, and maybe she had, to give the one who came next a chance. I like to think she knew who that was: the one who'd been running things all along.

That trap may sound familiar. You built the effect, and it works, and that's exactly what makes it hard to change: people come for it, and you're good at it. A bartender in Havana, by one account, named a cocktail for the star, light and sweet, a drink for the curls. The cocktail I've made for you is for the one behind them. The rum leads now, the lime keeps it dry, and the grenadine is homemade, from real pomegranate with thyme steeped in it. It's made at home, by you, as a nod to the one who made the image.

A hard year shouldn't be what makes the change for you. Choose the next version of yourself while the choice is still yours, and let a few people watch you choose. Some will miss the old one for a while. The ones who stay will be the ones who wanted you, and that's the company you've been missing.
